mn102:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn102:1.3: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
mn102:1.5: “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
mn102:2.1: “Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speculate about the future, who hold views about the future, and who assert various propositions concerning the future.
mn102:2.2: ‘The self is percipient and free from disease after death’—
mn102:2.4: ‘the self is non-percipient and free from disease after death’—
mn102:2.6: ‘the self is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient and free from disease after death’—
mn102:2.8: or else they declare[^1] the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being, or some assert Nibbāna here and now.[^2]
mn102:2.9: So (a) they declare an existing self to be free from disease after death, or (b) they declare the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being, or (c) some assert Nibbāna here and now.
mn102:2.10: So these five become three, and these three become five—
mn102:2.11: this is the summary of the five and the three.
mn102:3.1: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless, or they declare it percipient of unity, or they declare it percipient of diversity, or they declare it percipient of the limited, or they declare it percipient of the measureless; or else, going beyond all this, some assert the totality of consciousness,[^3] as measureless and imperturbable.
mn102:4.2: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless, or they declare it percipient of unity, or they declare it percipient of diversity, or they declare it percipient of the limited, or they declare it percipient of the measureless, or else there is that perception which is declared to be the purest, the highest, the supreme, the unsurpassed of those perceptions—
mn102:4.3: whether perceptions of form, or perceptions of the formless, or perceptions of unity, or perceptions of diversity.
mn102:4.4: ‘There is nothing’—some assert the base of nothingness, as measureless and imperturbable.
mn102:4.5: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’[^4]
mn102:4.6: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:5.1: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.
mn102:6.1: Now, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—these oppose them.
mn102:6.3: ‘Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, non-perception.’
mn102:7.2: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.
mn102:7.3: For, bhikkhus, if any ascetic or brahmin were to say:
mn102:7.4: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I shall describe the coming or going, the passing away or reappearance, the growth, increase, or maturing of consciousness’—
mn102:7.6: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:7.7: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:8.1: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.
mn102:9.1: Now, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—these oppose them, and those ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—these too oppose them.
mn102:9.3: ‘Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart; non-perception is delusion; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely,
mn102:10.2: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—those good ascetics and brahmins declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self free from disease after death to be possessed of form, or they declare it to be formless, or they declare it to be both possessed of form and formless, or they declare it to be neither possessed of form nor formless.
mn102:10.3: For, bhikkhus, when any ascetics or brahmins declare the attainment of this base merely in terms of what has been seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, this is declared, bhikkhus, to be a disaster for the attainment of this base.
mn102:10.4: For this base, bhikkhus, is not declared to be attainable by an attainment accompanied by formations;
mn102:10.5: this base, bhikkhus, is declared to be attainable by an attainment accompanied by the residue of formations.
mn102:10.6: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:10.7: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:11.1: Now, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who declare the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being—those ascetics and brahmins who declare a percipient self to be free from disease after death—these oppose them; those ascetics and brahmins who declare a non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—these too oppose them; and those ascetics and brahmins who declare a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self to be free from disease after death—these too oppose them.
mn102:11.3: All these good ascetics and brahmins, being intent on what lies ahead, assert only attachment thus:
mn102:11.4: ‘So we shall be after death, so we shall be after death.’
mn102:12.1: Just as a merchant going about his trade thinks:
mn102:12.2: ‘From this I shall get that, with this I shall obtain that’;
mn102:12.3: so too, these good ascetics and brahmins seem, as it were, like merchants:
mn102:12.4: ‘So we shall be after death, so we shall be after death.’
mn102:12.6: Those good ascetics and brahmins who declare the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being—out of fear of individual existence, out of disgust with individual existence, they run and circle round that very individual existence.
mn102:12.7: Just as a dog tied by a leash and bound to a strong post or pillar runs and circles round that very post or pillar,
mn102:12.8: so too, these good ascetics and brahmins, out of fear of individual existence, out of disgust with individual existence, run and circle round that very individual existence.
mn102:12.9: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:12.10: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:13.1: Whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be, bhikkhus, who speculate about the future, who hold views about the future, and who assert various propositions concerning the future—all of them assert one or another of these five bases.
mn102:14.1: There are, bhikkhus, some ascetics and brahmins who speculate about the past, who hold views about the past, and who assert various propositions concerning the past.
mn102:14.2: ‘The self and the world are eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—[^5]
mn102:14.3: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.4: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are both eternal and not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.5: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.6: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are finite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.7: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are infinite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.8: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are both finite and infinite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.9: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.10: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of unity, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.11: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of diversity, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.12: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of the limited, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.13: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are percipient of the measureless, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.14: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are exclusively happy, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.15: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are exclusively suffering, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.16: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are both happy and suffering, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:14.17: thus some assert; ‘the self and the world are neither suffering nor happy, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—
mn102:15.1: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn102:15.2: ‘the self and the world are eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—that they should have, apart from faith, apart from liking, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it,[^6] any personal, purified, and clear knowledge of this—that is not possible.
mn102:15.3: But, bhikkhus, when there is no personal, purified, and clear knowledge, then even the mere fragment of knowledge that those good ascetics and brahmins clarify in that respect is itself declared to be clinging on the part of those good ascetics and brahmins.
mn102:15.4: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:15.5: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:16.1: Now, bhikkhus, of these, those ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn102:16.2: ‘the self and the world are not eternal, only this is true, everything else is wrong’ …
mn102:16.3: ‘the self and the world are both eternal and not eternal’ …
mn102:16.4: ‘the self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal’ …
mn102:16.5: ‘the self and the world are finite’ …
mn102:16.6: ‘the self and the world are infinite’ …
mn102:16.7: ‘the self and the world are both finite and infinite’ …
mn102:16.8: ‘the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite’ …
mn102:16.9: ‘the self and the world are percipient of unity’ …
mn102:16.10: ‘the self and the world are percipient of diversity’ …
mn102:16.11: ‘the self and the world are percipient of the limited’ …
mn102:16.12: ‘the self and the world are percipient of the measureless’ …
mn102:16.13: ‘the self and the world are exclusively happy’ …
mn102:16.14: ‘the self and the world are exclusively suffering’ …
mn102:16.15: ‘the self and the world are both happy and suffering’ …
mn102:16.16: ‘the self and the world are neither suffering nor happy, only this is true, everything else is wrong’—that they should have, apart from faith, apart from liking, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, any personal, purified, and clear knowledge of this—that is not possible.
mn102:16.17: But, bhikkhus, when there is no personal, purified, and clear knowledge, then even the mere fragment of knowledge that those good ascetics and brahmins clarify in that respect is itself declared to be clinging on the part of those good ascetics and brahmins.
mn102:16.18: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:16.19: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:17.1: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all[^7] upon the fetters of sensual desire, enters upon and abides in the joy of seclusion,[^8] (thinking:)
mn102:17.2: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in the joy of seclusion.’
mn102:17.3: That joy of seclusion of his ceases.
mn102:17.4: With the cessation of the joy of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of the grief, the joy of seclusion arises.
mn102:18.1: Just as, bhikkhus, when the shade departs, the sunlight spreads, and when the sunlight departs, the shade spreads;
mn102:18.2: so too, bhikkhus, with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of the grief, the joy of seclusion arises.
mn102:18.4: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, enters upon and abides in the joy of seclusion, (thinking:)
mn102:18.5: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in the joy of seclusion.’
mn102:18.6: That joy of seclusion of his ceases.
mn102:18.7: With the cessation of the joy of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of the grief, the joy of seclusion arises.
mn102:18.8: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:18.9: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:19.1: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, enters upon and abides in unworldly pleasure,[^9] (thinking:)
mn102:19.2: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in unworldly pleasure.’
mn102:19.3: That unworldly pleasure of his ceases.
mn102:19.4: With the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, the joy of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, unworldly pleasure arises.
mn102:20.1: Just as, bhikkhus, when the shade departs, the sunlight spreads, and when the sunlight departs, the shade spreads;
mn102:20.2: so too, bhikkhus, with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, the joy of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, unworldly pleasure arises.
mn102:20.4: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, enters upon and abides in unworldly pleasure, (thinking:)
mn102:20.5: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in unworldly pleasure.’
mn102:20.6: That unworldly pleasure of his ceases.
mn102:20.7: With the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, the joy of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the joy of seclusion, unworldly pleasure arises.
mn102:20.8: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:20.9: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:21.1: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, enters upon and abides in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,[^10] (thinking:)
mn102:21.2: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn102:21.3: That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of his ceases.
mn102:21.4: With the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises; with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
mn102:22.1: Just as, bhikkhus, when the shade departs, the sunlight spreads, and when the sunlight departs, the shade spreads;
mn102:22.2: so too, bhikkhus, with the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises; with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
mn102:22.4: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, enters upon and abides in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, (thinking:)
mn102:22.5: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I enter upon and abide in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
mn102:22.6: That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of his ceases.
mn102:22.7: With the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly pleasure arises; with the cessation of the unworldly pleasure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
mn102:22.8: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:22.9: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:23.1: Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, through surmounting neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, regards himself thus:
mn102:23.2: ‘I am at peace, I am quenched, I am without clinging.’
mn102:24.2: This good ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views based on the past and the relinquishing of views based on the future, through not resolving at all upon the fetters of sensual desire, through surmounting the joy of seclusion, through surmounting unworldly pleasure, through surmounting neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, regards himself thus:
mn102:24.3: ‘I am at peace, I am quenched, I am without clinging’;
mn102:24.4: certainly this venerable one asserts a way that is conducive to Nibbāna.
mn102:24.5: And yet this good ascetic or brahmin, clinging to a view based on the past, clings; clinging to a view based on the future, clings; clinging to the fetter of sensual desire, clings; clinging to the joy of seclusion, clings; clinging to unworldly pleasure, clings; clinging to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, clings.
mn102:24.6: And as for this venerable one’s regarding himself thus:
mn102:24.7: ‘I am at peace, I am quenched, I am without clinging’—this too is declared to be clinging on the part of this good ascetic or brahmin.
mn102:24.8: ‘This is conditioned and gross; but there is the cessation of formations—that exists.’
mn102:24.9: Knowing this thus, and seeing the escape from it, a Tathāgata has gone beyond it.
mn102:25.1: Now this, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely—
mn102:25.2: liberation without clinging, through knowing as it actually is the origin, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases of contact.”
mn102:25.3: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn102:25.4: Those bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
